rationale: A wins because it separates the hard stories instead of mashing them into one respectable-looking blur. A's "Sweetgreen's robot line runs at a better margin than its people line — and the company still isn't profitable" gives a finance reporter a real testable tension, then names the margin bridge, capex, sample size, and comparability proof. B is competent, but "Sweetgreen's own rollout is a concrete, citable case of reduced staff hours tied to automated assembly" turns a worry into a fact, which is how a pitch gets killed in the first fact-check.
gaps_in_A: "The prevailing belief is that a company that hasn't reached profitability should be conserving capital" asserts an investor consensus the update does not supply. Make it a question unless you have analyst notes or investor quotes.
"That's the decision other operators are weighing right now" widens one company's retrofit plan into an industry debate without evidence. It may be true, but it is not in the fact pack.
"tearing up existing stores" is vivid, but retrofit does not automatically mean major demolition, downtime, or heavy construction. Keep the color after you have the build-out details.
gaps_in_B: "Sweetgreen's own rollout is a concrete, citable case of reduced staff hours tied to automated assembly" is the bad miss. The update says some worry about reduced staff hours; it does not say hours were reduced.
"makes robot-assembled bowls the default, not the pilot" overstates "most new stores" into a cleaner narrative than the facts allow. Good headline, loose footing.

The finance angle collapses two possible stories: "margin lifts but net loss remains" and "is capex the right allocation before profitability." A separates those; B leaves sharper angles on the floor.

The proof list misses the nastiest reporting question: are automated stores comparable to traditional stores by age, market, site quality, and volume? Without that, the margin claim is a dressed-up confound.
